title: How Jaime Johnson's Shared Reading Leads to Vibrant Discussion
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Lemov uses a video of Jaime Johnson's sixth grade class at Bay Creek Middle School in Gwinnett County reading Grace Lin's Where The Mountain Meets the Moon to make an argument about why in-class shared reading produces better discussion than reading assigned as homework. He first inventories the craft on display: an annotation task that primes students to notice the thing they will later be asked to discuss, expressive teacher modelling that builds prosody, gentle prompts on tricky phrases, and students self-correcting into phrasing without being told. The theoretical core is working memory. Because it holds only one or two substantive ideas and decays within seconds, discussion that follows reading by a day or a night is discussion about a faded trace, and Lemov illustrates the decay with the familiar experience of losing a six digit authentication code the moment you get distracted. In Johnson's room the discussion sits seconds after the reading, so the material is still vivid, and the Turn and Talk both externalizes each student's thinking so it survives and lets students read the room to see whether their peers actually care what they say. He notes that even the speed of the transition matters, since going straight to whole-class discussion would let one long answer erase everyone else's insights. He closes by naming and rejecting the position of a friend who holds that English class is only for discussion and reading should happen elsewhere.
points: The annotation task is presented as a priming device: students are told in advance what to attend to, so the later discussion has material rather than needing to be manufactured.
Lemov's mechanism for why homework reading undercuts discussion is decay in working memory, made concrete by the six digit authentication code that vanishes if you pause to order a coffee.
Turn and Talk does two jobs at once, externalizing a student's thought so it is encoded, and letting the student gauge whether classmates will care about what they say.
Sequencing matters at the scale of seconds, since one classmate speaking for a minute before others share can erase the insights the others were holding.
Expressive oral reading is defended as fluency instruction, on the grounds that prosody reflecting understanding transfers to silent reading.
quotes: Not only should students read great books cover to cover, they should read them together, in class, often aloud.
Among other things we can use shared reading to rebuild attentional habits so that students experience 8 or 10 or 12 minutes of uninterrupted and undistracted text several times a day.
If she can get them to read aloud with prosody—expression that reflects understanding—research tells us it will help make them more fluent and expressive readers even when they read silently.
But the Turn and Talk also affords them the opportunity to read the room, to ask: If I’m called on the speak about the book will my classmates want me to speak? Will they care about what I say?

One of the things we know about working memory, the mental space where people hold ideas that they wish to think about, is that it is both small and fleeting. We can hold one or two ideas of substance in our working memory. And we start to forget what’s there within a few seconds.
Too often the things we want students to discuss are already fading to gray in their memory by the time we get around to it…. a bit like a six-digit code they were sent an hour ago.

But in Jamie’s classroom, students’ memory of the book is live and in vibrant color in their working memory. They remember more and with more depth and emotion because the discussion is so proximate to the experience of reading it…

I have a friend I admire who says that English class is only for discussion. There’s too much to do and so the reading should happen at home or outside the classroom. I would argue that he is profoundly wrong.
